claims.text: A blog post titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
AWS CDK allows developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
SST's Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation, and once stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine and bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
The SST team has said repeatedly, since the rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported architecture since.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST docs ('What is SST') say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published package.json of SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, and a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

The SST repository is now at `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`), and platform/package.json lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.

In SST's deploy chain, components compile into Pulumi resource declarations; the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations; Terraform-bridged providers translate resources into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine handles dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs underneath SST.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools in the same way SST embeds the engine.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Cross-reference links target /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, and /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric and Defang, like SST, rely on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath a narrower, more opinionated interface.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its Terraform providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package gets roughly 796,000 downloads per week (796,291 for September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has a larger GitHub star count than SST itself.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed, and its release cadence is unchanged by the team's work on opencode.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides centrally enforced guardrails, and components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components can be used with SST without leaving the Pulumi engine.
Linked pages exist: /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/.
SST does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across multiple applications on its own.
